topic: Irritable bowel syndrome and chronic diarrhoea
page_contents_html:
Irritable bowel syndrome and chronic diarrhoea

This pathway provides a single primary-care approach to persistent loose stool and suspected IBS. It supports a positive diagnosis of IBS while identifying patients who need investigation or referral for cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, coeliac disease, infection or malabsorption.

Two key testing messages

  • Include HIV serology in the initial GP blood panel for chronic diarrhoea.
  • Do not request faecal calprotectin routinely for every possible IBS presentation. Use it selectively after a negative qFIT when diarrhoea persists and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care assessment
accordion_sections.html:
History and examination

  • Duration, stool frequency and form, abdominal pain, bloating, urgency, incontinence, blood or mucus
  • Nocturnal symptoms, unintentional weight loss, fever and effect on daily function
  • Recent antibiotics, travel, infection exposure, diet and alcohol
  • Previous bowel or gallbladder surgery, pancreatitis or radiotherapy
  • Family history of colorectal or ovarian cancer, inflammatory bowel disease or coeliac disease
  • Medicines that may cause diarrhoea, including laxatives, metformin, PPIs, NSAIDs, SSRIs and magnesium-containing products

Examine for dehydration, weight loss, anaemia, abdominal mass, perianal disease and faecal impaction or overflow. Perform rectal examination where clinically indicated.

Rome IV criteria for a positive IBS diagnosis

IBS can be diagnosed when there is recurrent abdominal pain, on average at least 1 day per week in the last 3 months, associated with at least 2 of:

  • Related to defaecation
  • A change in stool frequency
  • A change in stool form

Symptoms should have started at least 6 months before diagnosis. Bloating, urgency, mucus, incomplete evacuation and symptoms made worse by eating may support the diagnosis.

Alarm features

  • Rectal bleeding
  • Unintentional weight loss
  • Abdominal or rectal mass
  • Anaemia
  • Frequent nocturnal symptoms
  • Family history of colorectal or ovarian cancer

New IBS-type symptoms in women aged 50 or over

If symptoms are new within the last 12 months, investigate for ovarian cancer in line with the current suspected-cancer pathway, including CA125 and pelvic ultrasound where indicated.

accordion_sections.heading: Initial investigations
accordion_sections.html:
Blood tests

  • FBC
  • CRP, or ESR/plasma viscosity
  • Coeliac serology: tissue transglutaminase antibody with total IgA
  • TFT
  • Other routine bloods according to the presentation
  • HIV serology when investigating chronic diarrhoea

Stool tests

  • qFIT in line with the current lower gastrointestinal symptoms pathway
  • Stool culture and other infection testing when clinically indicated
  • Ova, cysts and parasites when exposure or travel history makes this relevant
  • Faecal calprotectin only when the criteria below are met

If coeliac serology is positive, refer for gastroenterology assessment and confirmation. Advise the patient to continue eating gluten until assessment is complete.

Faecal calprotectin: use selectively

Consider faecal calprotectin only when all of the following apply:

  • There is persistent diarrhoea or loose stool and inflammatory bowel disease remains a realistic differential
  • qFIT is negative and colorectal cancer is not suspected
  • An infective cause has been considered and investigated where appropriate
  • The result will change management or the need for gastroenterology assessment

BSG guidance particularly supports faecal calprotectin in patients aged under 45 with diarrhoea where inflammatory bowel disease needs to be excluded.

Do not request it routinely for every patient meeting IBS criteria, for clear IBS-C, for stable established IBS, or as a colorectal cancer test.

Interpret the result using the current NHS Dumfries & Galloway laboratory comment and local action thresholds. Infection and medicines including NSAIDs can cause raised results.

accordion_sections.heading: Clinical decision after initial assessment
accordion_sections.html:
• Possible colorectal or ovarian cancer: use the current suspected-cancer pathway. Faecal calprotectin does not exclude cancer.
  • Possible inflammatory bowel disease: refer to gastroenterology when supported by symptoms and inflammatory markers or faecal calprotectin.
  • Positive coeliac serology: refer for specialist confirmation; the patient should continue eating gluten.
  • Identified infection or medicine-related diarrhoea: treat the cause and review.
  • Rome IV criteria met, no alarm features and satisfactory investigations: make a positive diagnosis of IBS and begin primary-care management.
  • Persistent diarrhoea without a clear diagnosis: refer after completing the initial work-up, including HIV serology.

accordion_sections.heading: Primary care management of IBS
accordion_sections.html:
Explain the diagnosis, agree the main symptoms to target and provide planned follow-up. Signpost to NHS Inform: IBS.

Lifestyle and diet

  • Regular meals, adequate fluid and regular physical activity
  • Reduce excess caffeine, alcohol and fizzy drinks
  • Adjust fibre according to symptoms; soluble fibre such as oats or ispaghula is usually better tolerated than bran
  • Consider a 4-week probiotic trial and stop if there is no benefit
  • Refer to dietetics if symptoms persist despite general advice; exclusion diets, including low FODMAP, should be supervised by a clinician with dietary expertise

Medication according to the predominant symptom

  • Pain or bloating: consider an antispasmodic as required.
  • IBS-D: loperamide is the first-choice antimotility medicine. Titrate to a soft, formed stool (Bristol type 4).
  • IBS-C: consider a laxative, avoiding lactulose where possible. Linaclotide may be considered when optimal or maximum tolerated doses of previous laxatives have failed and constipation has been present for at least 12 months; review after 3 months.
  • Persistent pain: if laxatives, loperamide or antispasmodics have not helped, consider a low-dose tricyclic antidepressant. Start at the equivalent of amitriptyline 5-10 mg at night and titrate if needed, usually not above 30 mg. This is an off-label indication: discuss and document informed consent. Review after 4 weeks and then every 6-12 months.

Consider cognitive behavioural therapy, hypnotherapy or psychological therapy when symptoms remain refractory after 12 months of appropriate treatment.

accordion_sections.heading: Who to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Urgent or suspected-cancer assessment

Use the appropriate current pathway for rectal bleeding, unexplained iron-deficiency anaemia, abdominal or rectal mass, significant unintentional weight loss, a concerning qFIT result, severe dehydration or acute systemic illness.

Refer to gastroenterology

  • Suspected inflammatory bowel disease
  • Positive coeliac serology
  • Persistent chronic diarrhoea with diagnostic uncertainty after the initial assessment
  • Evidence of malabsorption, pancreatic disease or another condition requiring specialist investigation
  • A clearly raised faecal calprotectin, or a persistently borderline result with compatible symptoms, using current local laboratory guidance
  • Severe or refractory IBS with a major effect on physical or psychological health, work, education or daily function despite appropriate primary care and specialist AHP input
  • The patient requests specialist review after an informed discussion

For chronic diarrhoea, include symptom duration and pattern, weight trend, medication review, relevant examination, qFIT, faecal calprotectin if indicated, stool microbiology and all blood results including HIV serology.

Refer to dietetics or another specialist AHP

Persistent IBS symptoms despite first-line advice should usually receive specialist dietary or other AHP input before medical gastroenterology referral, according to local service availability. For patients aged under 40 with satisfactory chronic diarrhoea assessment and IBS-D symptoms, consider gastroenterology dietetic input in line with the current local pathway.

accordion_sections.heading: Who not to refer
accordion_sections.html:
Specialist medical referral is usually unnecessary when:

  • Rome IV criteria are met, there are no alarm features and initial investigations are satisfactory
  • Symptoms are stable or improving with explanation, dietary measures or first-line medication
  • There is established IBS with no significant change in symptoms or new alarm feature
  • A reversible medicine, dietary or short-lived infective cause has been identified and symptoms settle after intervention

Do not arrange routine colonoscopy, ultrasound, hydrogen breath testing, repeated inflammatory markers or repeated faecal calprotectin solely to reassure a patient with a secure positive diagnosis of IBS.

accordion_sections.heading: Further investigation usually directed by secondary care
accordion_sections.html:
• Malabsorption: iron, B12, folate, calcium, albumin and faecal elastase as indicated
  • Immunodeficiency: immunoglobulins; confirm that primary-care HIV testing has been completed
  • Microscopic colitis: colonoscopy with biopsies
  • Inflammatory bowel disease: endoscopic assessment guided by symptoms and faecal calprotectin
  • Pancreatic exocrine insufficiency: faecal elastase and pancreatic imaging when indicated
  • Bile acid diarrhoea: specialist testing or treatment according to local practice
  • Lactose intolerance or small intestinal bacterial overgrowth: breath testing or specialist-directed treatment where appropriate

notes_for_editor: This is a comparison draft combining the IBS and chronic diarrhoea pathways; the two separate drafts remain available in the viewer.
The shared assessment and investigation sections remove duplication while the clinical decision section separates IBS management from causes needing referral.
Numerical faecal calprotectin thresholds remain deliberately omitted pending confirmation of the current D&G laboratory interpretive ranges.
Confirm the current local dietetic/AHP route, the under-40 dietetic recommendation, stool microbiology details and linaclotide formulary position before publication.
